ph-and-pka-s1.title: Four acid-base indicators
ph-and-pka-s1.text: Each indicator is a weak acid, HIn, whose protonated and deprotonated forms have different colors.

ph-and-pka-s2.title: One acid in three buffers
ph-and-pka-s2.html: Key: HA the protonated form of a weak acid with pKa 6.0; A⁻ the deprotonated form. The three boxes are at pH 5.0, 6.0 and 7.0, in some order. Water and buffer ions are not drawn.

ph-and-pka-s3.title: An amino acid in solution
ph-and-pka-s3.html:
Glycine has a carboxylic acid group and an amine group: H₃N⁺–CH₂–COOH in strongly acidic solution.

pKa of the –COOH group: 2.3. pKa of the –NH₃⁺ group: 9.6.

items.q: Acetic acid is titrated with NaOH; the equivalence point is at pH 8.72. Which indicator is the best choice?
options: Phenolphthalein
Bromothymol blue
Bromocresol green
Methyl orange

why.correct: An indicator changes color over about pKa ± 1. Phenolphthalein (pKa 9.3) changes between about 8.3 and 10.3, which brackets the equivalence pH of 8.72 on the steep part of the curve.
options: Right: its color change falls on the steep rise around pH 8.7.
Its range (about 6.1 to 8.1) sits just below the equivalence pH; it would change a little early, though on a steep curve the error is small. Phenolphthalein matches better.
Its range (about 3.7 to 5.7) is in the buffer region; it would change color long before equivalence.
It changes near pH 3.5, at the very start of the titration.

items.q: Ammonia is titrated with HCl; the equivalence point is at pH 5.28. Which indicator is the best choice?
options: Bromocresol green
Phenolphthalein
Bromothymol blue
Methyl orange

why.correct: Bromocresol green (pKa 4.7) changes between about 3.7 and 5.7, which brackets the acidic equivalence pH of 5.28.
options: Right: pKa close to the equivalence pH.
Phenolphthalein changes near pH 9, in the buffer region of this titration, long before equivalence.
It changes near pH 7, before equivalence in this titration of a weak base.
Its range ends near 4.5, below the equivalence pH; it would change late, after the steep drop.

items.q: What color is bromothymol blue in a solution at pH 9.5?
options: Blue
Yellow
Green
Colorless

why.correct: pH 9.5 is well above its pKa of 7.1, so the deprotonated form, In⁻ (blue), predominates.
options: Right: pH > pKa, the deprotonated form.
Yellow is the HIn form, which predominates below pH 7.1.
Green, a mix of both forms, appears only near pH 7.1.
Neither form of bromothymol blue is colorless.

items.q: In a solution at pH 5.4, what is the ratio [In⁻]/[HIn] for bromocresol green?

mistakes.why: Value: that is [HIn]/[In⁻]. pH is above pKa, so the deprotonated form In⁻ is in the majority and the ratio is above 1.

why.correct: From Ka = [H₃O⁺][In⁻]/[HIn]: [In⁻]/[HIn] = Ka/[H₃O⁺] = 10^(pH − pKa) = 10^(5.4 − 4.7) = 10^0.7 = 5. (One significant figure: the exponent 0.7 has one decimal place.)

items.q: A strong acid is titrated with a strong base (equivalence at pH 7.00, with a very steep rise from about pH 4 to 10). Which indicators would give an accurate end point? Select all that apply.
options: Bromothymol blue
Phenolphthalein
Bromocresol green
Methyl orange

why.correct: Near the equivalence point of a strong-strong titration, one drop moves the pH across several units, so any indicator whose range lies inside the steep part works. Bromothymol blue (about 6 to 8) and phenolphthalein (about 8 to 10) do.
options: Right: centered on pH 7.
Right: within the steep rise; the volume error is a fraction of a drop.
Its range starts near pH 3.7, below the steep part, so it would change slightly early.
It changes near pH 3 to 4.5, before the steep rise.
Box 3
Box 1
Box 2
Box 2, which has equal amounts

why.correct: At pH 7.0, one unit above pKa, [A⁻]/[HA] = 10^(7.0 − 6.0) = 10, which matches 9 A⁻ to 1 HA (about 10 : 1).
options: Right: pH > pKa, mostly deprotonated.
Box 1 is mostly HA, which fits pH 5.0, below pKa.
Box 2 has equal amounts, which fits pH = pKa = 6.0.
Equal amounts mean pH = pKa = 6.0, not 7.0.

items.q: Box 1 is brought to pH 3.0 by adding a strong acid. How does the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] change?
options: It falls to about 1/1000
It rises to about 1000
It stays about 1/10
It falls to about 1/3

why.correct: [A⁻]/[HA] = 10^(pH − pKa) = 10^(3.0 − 6.0) = 10⁻³: nearly all the acid is protonated.
options: Right: three units below pKa.
Lower pH means more H₃O⁺, which protonates A⁻; the ratio falls.
The ratio depends on pH; it changes as the pH changes.
The ratio changes by a factor of ten per pH unit, not in proportion to the pH value.

items.q: At pH 5.0, what percentage of the acid is in the A⁻ form?

mistakes.why: Value: a ratio of 1 : 10 means 1 part A⁻ in 11 parts total, not 1 in 10. Percent = 1/(1 + 10) × 100.

why.correct: [A⁻]/[HA] = 10^(5.0 − 6.0) = 0.10, so for every 10 HA there is 1 A⁻. Fraction A⁻ = 1/(1 + 10) = 0.091, which is 9.1%.

items.q: A medicine is absorbed through cell membranes only in its uncharged form, HA (pKa 6.0). In which region would it be absorbed best?
options: The stomach, at pH 2
The small intestine, at pH 7
Blood, at pH 7.4
Blood and the stomach equally, at pH 7.4 and 2

why.correct: At pH 2, four units below pKa, the drug is almost entirely HA (the uncharged form), so the most of it can cross membranes.
options: Right: pH far below pKa, protonated form predominates.
At pH 7, one unit above pKa, most of the drug is A⁻, which is charged.
At pH 7.4, about 96% of the drug is A⁻.
The fraction in the HA form depends strongly on pH: about 4% at pH 7.4 but nearly 100% at pH 2.

items.q: Which form of glycine predominates at pH 7?
options: H₃N⁺–CH₂–COO⁻
H₃N⁺–CH₂–COOH
H₂N–CH₂–COO⁻
H₂N–CH₂–COOH

why.correct: pH 7 is above 2.3, so the –COOH group is mostly deprotonated (–COO⁻); pH 7 is below 9.6, so the –NH₃⁺ group stays protonated.
options: Right: compare pH with each pKa separately.
At pH 7, well above 2.3, the –COOH group has lost its proton.
At pH 7, below 9.6, the amine group is still protonated.
This form would need pH above 9.6 for the amine and below 2.3 for the acid at once, which is impossible.

items.q: Which form of glycine predominates at pH 11?
options: H₂N–CH₂–COO⁻
H₃N⁺–CH₂–COO⁻
H₃N⁺–CH₂–COOH
H₂N–CH₂–COOH

why.correct: pH 11 is above both pKa values, so both groups are deprotonated: –COO⁻ and –NH₂.
options: Right: both groups deprotonated.
This is the form between pH 2.3 and 9.6.
This is the form below pH 2.3.
This form cannot predominate at any pH: the acid group loses its proton long before the amine group does.

items.q: At pH 3.00, what is the ratio [–COO⁻]/[–COOH] for glycine's carboxylic acid group? (Take its pKa as 2.30.)

mistakes.why: Value: pH is above pKa, so the deprotonated form is in the majority: 10^(pH − pKa) = 10^(+0.70), above 1.

why.correct: [A⁻]/[HA] = 10^(pH − pKa) = 10^(3.00 − 2.30) = 10^0.70 = 5.0. (Two decimal places in the exponent give two significant figures.)

items.q: A glycine solution at pH 7 is made more basic, to pH 10.5. Predict the change in each.

variables.name: Fraction of amine groups that are –NH₃⁺
variables.why: pH rises above the amine pKa of 9.6, so most –NH₃⁺ groups lose their proton.

variables.name: Fraction of acid groups that are –COO⁻
variables.why: At both pH 7 and 10.5 the pH is far above 2.3, so essentially all acid groups are already –COO⁻.

variables.name: pKa of the amine group
variables.why: pKa is a property of the group at a given temperature; pH changes do not change it.

why.correct: Each group follows its own pKa: the one whose pKa the pH crosses changes form; the other stays as it was.

items.q: A weak acid has pKa 4.2. In a solution at pH 2.2, which form predominates?
options: HA, by about 100 to 1
A⁻, by about 100 to 1
HA and A⁻ in equal amounts
A⁻, by about 2 to 1

why.correct: pH is 2 units below pKa: [A⁻]/[HA] = 10⁻², so HA outnumbers A⁻ about 100 to 1.
options: Right: pH below pKa, protonated form.
Below pKa, the protonated form predominates, not the deprotonated one.
Equal amounts happen only at pH = pKa.
This reads the pH difference as a ratio; the exponent is −2, so the factor is 100 in favor of HA.

items.q: Put these steps for choosing an indicator in order.
options: Decide what is in the flask at the equivalence point
Estimate the equivalence-point pH (7, above 7 or below 7)
Find an indicator whose pKa is close to that pH
Check that its range (pKa ± 1) falls on the steep part of the curve

why.correct: The species at equivalence set its pH; the indicator's pKa must match that pH so the color change coincides with the steep rise.

items.q: A student titrates acetic acid with NaOH using methyl orange (pKa 3.5) as the indicator. How will the measured volume of NaOH compare with the true equivalence volume?
options: Smaller, because the color changes early in the buffer region
Larger, because the color changes after the equivalence point
Equal, because any indicator marks the equivalence point
Larger, because methyl orange reacts with some of the NaOH

why.correct: Methyl orange turns from red to yellow by about pH 4.5. Acetic acid's curve passes that pH early in the buffer region, long before the equivalence volume, so the student stops too soon.
options: Right: the end point comes early, so too little base is recorded.
The color change happens at about pH 4.5, which comes before, not after, equivalence here.
An indicator marks the pH of its own pKa, which must match the equivalence pH.
The tiny amount of indicator uses a negligible amount of base; the problem is where its color changes.

items.q: Methylammonium, CH₃NH₃⁺, has pKa 10.64. What fraction of methylamine is in the protonated form at pH 9.64? Give your answer as a decimal.

mistakes.why: Value: that is the deprotonated fraction. pH is below pKa, so the protonated form CH₃NH₃⁺ is in the majority.
Value: one pH unit below pKa is a 10 : 1 ratio, not 100 : 1. Fraction = 10/(10 + 1).

why.correct: [B]/[BH⁺] = 10^(pH − pKa) = 10^(9.64 − 10.64) = 0.10, so 10 BH⁺ for each B. Protonated fraction = 10/(10 + 1) = 0.91.

items.q: A student says, "At pH 7 every weak acid is mostly deprotonated, because 7 is neutral." Which acid shows the claim is wrong?
options: HOCl, pKa 7.5
Acetic acid, pKa 4.74
HF, pKa 3.17
HNO₂, pKa 3.40

why.correct: Whether an acid is mostly deprotonated depends on pH compared with its pKa, not on 7. HOCl has pKa 7.5, so at pH 7 the protonated HOCl outnumbers OCl⁻ about 3 to 1.
options: Right: pH below pKa, so the protonated form predominates.
At pH 7, acetic acid is mostly acetate (pH above pKa), which agrees with the claim.
HF is mostly F⁻ at pH 7, which agrees with the claim.
HNO₂ is mostly NO₂⁻ at pH 7, which agrees with the claim.
